drills.q: Name the three years and authors behind hexagonal, onion, and clean architecture.
drills.a: Cockburn 2005 (hexagonal), Palermo 2008 (onion), Martin 2012 (clean). Same idea, different vocabulary.

drills.q: A code reviewer sees a domain object with only getters/setters and a service class named OrderService.cancelOrder(order). What's the diagnosis?
drills.a: Anaemic domain model -- behavior that should live on the Order entity (order.cancel()) has been pushed into an orchestrating service instead, a common failure mode of layered architecture with no enforced dependency direction.

drills.q: What is the one rule that hexagonal, onion, and clean architecture all enforce, regardless of naming?
drills.a: Dependencies point inward toward the domain; the domain defines interfaces for anything it needs from the outside (a database, an API), and outer layers implement those interfaces, never the reverse.

drills.q: You inherit a codebase with folders named orders/, inventory/, billing/, but orders/ directly queries inventory's tables via SQL join. Is this a modular monolith?
drills.a: No -- shared/joined tables across modules violate the no-shared-tables requirement. It's a monolith with folder names implying boundaries that aren't enforced.

drills.q: What 2026 statistic supports 'modular monolith by default' over 'microservices by default'?
drills.a: 42% of organizations that adopted microservices have consolidated some services back into larger units, with satisfaction down 19 points vs 2024 and infra costs reported 3.75x-6x higher for equivalent functionality.

drills.q: A team split their monolith into an auth-service, a validation-service, and a database-service. Diagnose the likely outcome.
drills.a: Chattiness anti-pattern: splitting along technical layers rather than business capability means a single business operation now fans out across multiple network hops for what used to be in-process calls, with none of the independent-deployability benefit real bounded-context splits provide.

drills.q: Five engineers own fifteen microservices, and every deploy requires coordinating across most of them. What is this, and what's the fix?
drills.a: A distributed monolith -- network cost of microservices without independent deployability. Fix: consolidate services with correlated release cadence and no real scaling divergence back into a modular monolith.

drills.q: State Conway's Law and the Inverse Conway Maneuver in one sentence each.
drills.a: Conway's Law: systems mirror the communication structure of the organizations that build them. Inverse Conway Maneuver: deliberately restructure teams to match your target architecture, since moving team boundaries is cheaper than holding a service boundary against actual communication patterns.

drills.q: Describe the strangler fig pattern for extracting a microservice, and its hardest part in practice.
drills.a: Route a growing percentage of traffic to the new service via a routing layer while the old path stays live, cut over once proven, then delete the old path -- always releasable. Hardest part: keeping data consistent between old and new paths during the transition, usually requiring outbox/CDC machinery.

drills.q: Give a concrete, defensible reason to split off a microservice from day one rather than starting with a modular monolith.
drills.a: A component with an inherently different scaling/cost profile known up front, e.g. a GPU-bound transcoding pipeline next to a CPU-bound web app, where co-locating would force over- or under-provisioning one side.

drills.q: How do you enforce a modular monolith's boundaries so they don't erode under deadline pressure?
drills.a: Tooling, not convention: fitness-function tests (ArchUnit + Spring Modulith in the JVM, import-linter in Python, dependency-cruiser in JS/TS) that fail the build on a cross-module internal import or a cross-module table join.

drills.q: When is hexagonal/onion/clean architecture NOT worth adopting?
drills.a: For a CRUD app with one datastore that will never realistically be swapped and thin domain logic -- the ports/adapters/use-case indirection costs more in navigation and boilerplate than it returns in testability or swappability.
